newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline, cattle, hog prices sharply higher.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline, cattle, hog prices sharply higher.

text.p: Gasoline prices ended sharply higher Tuesday, giving crude oil and heating oil prices a boost, as two refineries shut down gasoline producing units and bullish political news lifted the market.
Cattle and hog prices jumped on tight supplies and a pickup in cash market demand.
"Gasoline clearly was the leader here ... while heating oil and crude lagged," said Smith Barney analyst John Saucer.
Gasoline for October delivery ended 2.76 cents a gallon higher at 62.83 cents on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
October heating oil settled up 2.21 cents a gallon to 69.69 cents, while November crude oil rose 70 cents higher at $24.07 a barrel. The October contract in crude expired Friday.

The gasoline spot market firmed on news Coastal Corp. shut its 20,000 barrel-per-day catalytic cracking unit, used to make light oil products such as gasoline, in Corpus Christi, Texas, last Friday for maintenance. In Coffeyville, Kan., Farmland Industries Inc. took down a catalytic cracker at its refinery there for at least 10 days.

On the political front, doctors are set to decide Wednesday when they will operate on Russia's President Boris Yeltin, who faces heart surgery. The market fears Yeltsin's ailing health could create political instability in the region. Russia is one of the world's largest oil producers.

Meanwhile, General Mohsen Rezaei, commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted in the daily Tehran Times as saying Tehran would strongly retaliate throughout the Gulf against any aggressive moves by the United States or Israel.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, October live cattle closed 1.125 cents a pound higher at 72.725 cents. October live hogs closed 0.05 cent per pound higher at 57.225 cents after setting a life-of-contract high at 57.450 cents earlier.
February pork belly prices also finished strong at 77.50 cents per pound, up 0.85 cent. Pork bellies are the raw material for bacon, which has seen strong demand this year.
"There's good structural demand throughout the industry, not just in the fast food sector," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.

In cattle, a slowdown in slaughter since last week has been supporting wholesale beef prices. This in turn fuelled speculation that packers will raise bids for fed cattle as they work their way through the supplies they own.
Talk that the government's quarterly report on the population of hogs and pigs due on Friday will show tight hog supplies into early 1997 also fed buying of futures.
CME November lumber closed down $8.70 at $342.20 per thousand board feet on indications of weakening demand for lumber at retail outlets as summer ends.
"Retailers are just in no mood to buy" after having to pay high mill asking prices the past three months, said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
Tight coffee supplies for immediate delivery helped boost coffee futures. At the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa, December coffee ended 1.45 cent per pound higher at $1.06.

While a flood of newly harvested coffee from Central and South America points to lower prices in coming weeks, prompt supplies are still under strain, said Victor Henriquez, president of Miami-based trading firm Hencorp Becstone.
Steady buying from U.S. and European coffee roasters this week has underpinned the market in recent days, he added.
"Technically, the panorama is looking better," Henriquez said. "The market wants to pick up."
At the Commodity Exchange in New York, precious metals ended higher helped by the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision not to raise interest rates.
December gold ended up $1.30 an ounce at $385.70, and December silver gained 4.0 cents at $4.935 an ounce.
